overview: This file concerns Japanese iron, steel, and mining developments during the late 1930s. It opens with a 1935 cross-reference to a military attaché report about a secret Japanese high-speed ore-smelting process, followed by Department of State correspondence and filing material associated with mining representative John A. Savage. The principal document is Savage’s June 1938 memorandum on Japan’s expanding steel capacity in Manchukuo and its dependence on iron ore imported or developed in Manchuria, Korea, British Malaya, Australia, China, and the Philippines. It supplies unusually detailed estimates of plant capacity, ore reserves, grades, tonnages, freight costs, equipment contracts, and the potential use of British and American control over ore supplies as economic and military leverage against Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to military attaché report on Japanese ore-smelting process
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to Military Intelligence Division Report No. 8076 concerning a reportedly Japanese high-speed ore-smelting invention.
subfiles.summary: This administrative cross-reference points to a report filed under 894.20 M.I.D. Reports/42. The referenced report concerned a high-speed ore-smelting process said to have been invented by a Japanese person, although details of the process had not been made public.

subfiles.title: Jacobs letter to Savage concerning his memorandum and proposed Washington visit
subfiles.from: J. E. Jacobs, Chief, Office of Philippine Affairs
subfiles.about: Jacobs thanks Savage for his letter and memorandum, discusses the timing of a Washington visit, and reports Consul General Davis’s departure for Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: Jacobs acknowledges Savage’s recent letter and says that he read the enclosed memorandum with considerable interest. He asks Savage to reach Washington before July 1 because Jacobs will then begin a month’s leave. He also notes that Consul General M. B. Davis has departed for his new post in Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Office of Philippine Affairs file cover for Savage mining material
subfiles.from: Office of Philippine Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: The sheet records the filing and routing of John A. Savage & Co. material concerning mining and manganese under decimal file 894.6351/6-2238.
subfiles.summary: This administrative cover identifies John A. Savage and his Duluth firm and associates the material with the Office of Philippine Affairs and the Department of State’s mining classification. It repeats the file number several times and bears a later filing stamp dated October 25, 1951.

subfiles.title: Savage memorandum on Japan’s iron-ore supplies and steel expansion
subfiles.to: Office of Philippine Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Savage assesses Japan’s plans to expand steel production and its vulnerable dependence on iron-ore sources across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Savage describes plans by Nissan, Mitsubishi, German suppliers, and American engineers to enlarge the Shōwa works in Manchukuo from about 800,000 tons of steel ingots to an eventual 3.5 million tons. He surveys prospective and existing ore supplies in Manchuria, Korea, British Malaya, Australia, China, and the Philippines, giving estimates for reserves, grades, annual shipments, prices, and transportation costs. Australian export restrictions, Chinese labor resistance in Malaya, wartime disruption in China, and the rejection of Japanese interest in Surigao are presented as constraints on Japan’s supply. Savage concludes that Britain and the United States could undertake effective economic and military action by restricting these ores or doubling their delivered cost to Japan.

interest: The Savage memorandum is especially useful because it joins strategic analysis to detailed commercial and technical intelligence: steelmaking capacity, ore grades, reserve estimates, shipment volumes, delivered prices, infrastructure plans, and foreign equipment contracts all appear in a compact account. It maps Japan’s prewar heavy industry onto a transnational resource network stretching from Manchuria and Korea to Malaya, Australia, China, and the Philippines, while explicitly anticipating economic warfare through control of raw materials. The correspondence, cross-reference, and later filing marks also reveal how industrial intelligence circulated through the Military Attaché, the Office of Philippine Affairs, and the State Department’s decimal filing system.
